Why do dLLMs tend to collapse in RL
In previous discussions of dLLMs, the focus was often on how they differ from autoregressive models: one generates tokens from left to right, while the other gradually approaches a complete sequence through denoising. The probabilistic factorization of the former is naturally explicit, whereas the latter behaves more like repeatedly refining an answer within a continually shrinking space of uncertainty.
Yet once we move into the RL stage, this difference is no longer just a matter of modeling style. It becomes a direct optimization issue.

Why can dLLMs not simply do RL?

For a dLLM, the true log likelihood of a sequence sample x_0 requires marginalizing over all intermediate states along the entire unmask trajectory, which is an exponentially large and intractable computation.
log⁡pθ(x0)=log⁡∑x1:Tpθ(x0:T)=log⁡∑x1:Tpθ(xT)∏t=1Tpθ(xt−1∣xt)\log p_\theta(x_0)=\log\sum_{x_{1:T}} p_\theta(x_{0:T}) =\log\sum_{x_{1:T}} p_\theta(x_T)\prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)
The summation ranges over all possible discrete sequences x_1 through x_T at every step, and the state space grows exponentially with both sequence length and vocabulary size, making exact analytical evaluation or exhaustive enumeration impossible. In practice, research therefore introduces an ELBO
log⁡pθ(x0)≥Eq(x1:T∣x0)[log⁡pθ(x0:T)−log⁡q(x1:T∣x0)],\log p_\theta(x_0)\ge \mathbb{E}_{q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)}\Big[\log p_\theta(x_{0:T})-\log q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)\Big],
samples the forward process q, and uses it to estimate the right hand side as a computable lower bound.
However, this estimate depends on Monte Carlo sampling and typically has high variance. In particular, discrete variables do not have a reparameterization path comparable to continuous diffusion, so low variance unbiased gradient estimation is difficult.
As a result, obtaining a converged log likelihood or an accurate gradient requires many samples and elaborate variance reduction techniques, which is precisely the problem that VRPO aims to address.
For dLLMs, the likelihood of the entire sequence is often intractable, which means that the importance ratio relied upon by many RL methods cannot be obtained exactly. One can only estimate it through proxies such as ELBO or mean field approximations.
The problem is that once the ratio is no longer exact but becomes a noisy approximation, the policy update mechanism that is relatively stable in AR models can be amplified by this noise.
Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Language Models
The paper argues that the key to training collapse is not a single bad update, but a positive feedback loop: noisy ratio estimation induces sharp gradient spikes, these spikes push policy drift, and policy drift further increases the variance of subsequent ratio estimates, eventually driving the system into instability.
Standard GRPO often works well in AR settings because it assumes that policy probabilities are controllable, updates are interpretable, and clipping behaves reliably. In dLLMs, however, the authors point out two major issues with this logic.
  • First, conditional clipping is not sufficiently stable under noisy ratios. Updates that should have been clipped may bypass the trigger condition because of estimation error, allowing gradient magnitudes to remain inflated.
  • Second, fixed group size normalization is unsafe in a high variance environment because it does not adapt to the actual strength of the updates in the current batch, and may instead further magnify gradient fluctuations that are already unstable.
The idea behind StableDRL is straightforward. Since the problem arises from noisy ratios being incorrectly amplified, the optimization procedure should no longer depend on fragile conditional triggers, but instead be reformulated in a way that is robust to noise. The paper proposes two core methods.
The first is unconditional clipping, which removes the conditional mechanism and directly constrains the ratio so that extreme values are suppressed. The intuition is clear: when the reliability of the ratio is limited to begin with, it is better to be conservative than to let a few outliers distort the entire update.
The second is self normalization, which no longer relies on a fixed group size, but instead normalizes by the sum of clipped importance ratios. The significance of this design is that the update scale is no longer determined by a constant unrelated to the current noise level, but is instead tied to the effective information in the batch itself.
These two designs may look simple, but they address a very fundamental problem: how to keep RL updates under control when they are based on noisy proxy ratios. A central point made by the paper is that clipping alone is not enough, because it can only suppress extreme values and cannot solve the drift introduced by normalization itself. Self normalization alone is also insufficient, because without clipping the outliers in the ratio will merely be averaged rather than removed. Only by combining the two can the update truly be constrained to a stable range.
The authors even interpret this design as a geometric constraint on per sample gradients. Updates are no longer allowed to move arbitrarily through regions of high variance, but are restricted to a more controllable convex hull. Although this framing is theoretical, the intuition is easy to grasp. The goal is not to let the model learn more aggressively, but to prevent it from learning too strongly in the wrong direction.
Another noteworthy aspect of the paper is that it does not limit itself to full attention dLLMs. It further extends the method to block diffusion models, since dLLMs often perform better when they degenerate toward semi AR behavior. To address probability estimation in block models, the authors introduce staircase attention, which enables leakage free proxy estimation.
The key issue here is that if training in block diffusion is not handled carefully, the estimation procedure can easily leak future information, creating a mismatch between the training objective and the actual generation process. The role of staircase attention is to make the estimation procedure more strictly constrained, so that the proxy can support RL updates without violating the causal structure of diffusion generation. This design shows that the authors are not merely trying to make RL run, but are also trying to preserve consistency between the optimization procedure and the generative mechanism of the model.
For a long time, we have treated the ratio as a taken for granted intermediate quantity, assuming that once we have a proxy, we can simply continue using the conventional policy optimization framework. StableDRL reminds us that in dLLMs, the proxy ratio itself is already part of the system error and can no longer be handled in the same way as an exact likelihood. In other words, RL for dLLMs is not just about adopting a different generation scheme. It changes the statistical structure of the entire optimization problem.
I personally find this kind of theoretical work especially compelling, because benchmark chasing alone is ultimately meaningless. Rather than trying to eliminate noise or mismatch, it acknowledges that noise exists and incorporates it into the RL framework, then uses more suitable clipping and normalization rules to turn noise into a controllable approximation.
